title: What exactly is stoicism?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Stoicism: its origins in ancient Athens with Zeno of Citium (transcribed as Zeno of Sidium) and the Stoa Poikile, its compromise between Socratic and Cynic ideas, the goal of eudaimonia, the three areas of study (physics, logic, ethics), indifferents and the four cardinal virtues, key figures (Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus Aurelius, Cleanthes, Chrysippus), its transfer from Athens to Rome, modern uses (Albert Ellis and CBT, Admiral James Stockdale, Silicon Valley), negative visualization, and criticisms. The episode opens with tour dates and closes with a listener mail story about a drug-sniffing dog mistaken for a bomb dog.

segments.title: Tour dates announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce North American tour dates and a benefit show in Atlanta, with ticket info at sysklive.com.

segments.title: Opening banter and philosophy quizzes
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic, joke about philosophy quizzes, and discuss why Stoicism is appealing today as a practical blueprint for living.

segments.title: Popular meaning of stoic and emotional control
segments.summary: The hosts contrast the everyday meaning of 'stoic' as grim endurance with actual Stoicism, which teaches emotional control and focusing only on what one can change.

segments.title: Zeno and the Stoa Poikile
segments.summary: Zeno of Citium founds Stoicism after a shipwreck, drawing on Cynic ideas and the painted porch in Athens where people gathered to talk.

segments.title: Eudaimonia, Socrates, and the Cynics
segments.summary: Stoicism is presented as a compromise between Socratic virtue ethics and Cynic rejection of wealth, with the goal of eudaimonia, a flourishing life. Wealth is treated as acceptable but not something to be attached to.

segments.title: Work, happiness, and modern relevance
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how changing work life, including remote work, may fuel renewed interest in Stoicism, and the criticism that philosophy can be self-indulgent introspection.

segments.title: Early Stoics and transmission to Rome
segments.summary: Early Stoics including Cleanthes, Chrysippus-era figures, Seneca, and Epictetus are named, and the philosophy moves from Athens to Rome. Epictetus, a former slave, and his Enchiridion are discussed.

segments.title: Physics, logic, and ethics
segments.summary: The three areas of Stoic study are explained: physics (the natural world and interconnection), logic (reason and epistemology), and ethics.

segments.title: Indifferents and the four cardinal virtues
segments.summary: Only the four virtues are good under all circumstances. Wealth and disease are 'indifferents' that may be preferred or dispreferred. Adversity is reframed as an opportunity for growth.

segments.title: Negative visualization and criticism
segments.summary: Negative visualization, imagining the worst case, is explained with a child's-illness example. Cicero's criticism of Stoicism as dampening enthusiasm is mentioned, along with the contrast with positive thinking.

segments.title: Modern applications: CBT, Stockdale, and critiques
segments.summary: Albert Ellis and cognitive behavioral therapy are linked to Epictetus. Admiral James Stockdale credits Stoicism for surviving Vietnam POW captivity. Critiques include its appeal to the wealthy and as a potential pacifier for social change.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the Stoicism overview as a starting point and say goodbye.

segments.title: Listener mail: bomb dog finds drugs
segments.summary: Listener Eric Stover describes a bomb-sniffing dog that alerted on an employee's locker at a New York concert and turned out to contain drugs.
